source_text: Numquid de Adam operibus interrogatus eras, aut quaesitum fuerat, utrum ille voluntate peccasset? Quod quidem contra te mox quaeretur. Esto, aliis te delectet illudere; cuius deformitatis est, ut tu tibimet imponas? Quippe haud mihi valeo persuadere, quod tantam deformitatem non fraude, sed opinione patiaris. In uno eodemque versu assentiris, non posse esse sine voluntate delictum, et subdis protinus, peccatum quod sine motu animi libero manere non dixeras, in omnibus hominibus sine voluntate regnare.
pass_a_gloss: Had you been asked about Adam's works, or had it been inquired whether he had sinned by will? Which indeed will soon be asked against you. Be it that it delights you to mock others; of what deformity is it that you impose on yourself? For I cannot persuade myself that you suffer so great a deformity not by fraud but by opinion. In one and the same verse you assent that there cannot be offense without will, and you immediately subjoin that the sin which you had not said remains without a free motion of the mind reigns in all humans without will.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS opus; Blaise God's works vs devil's
proper name; first human in Julian's anti-tradux argument

pass_b_english: Had you been asked about Adam’s actions, or whether he sinned by his will? That question will indeed soon be put against you. Granted, you enjoy deceiving others; but how ugly it is to deceive yourself! Yet I cannot persuade myself that you suffer such ugliness from conviction rather than fraud. In one and the same line you agree that an offense cannot exist without will, then immediately add that the sin which you said could not subsist without a free movement of mind reigns in all human beings without will.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
